notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on limitation and retrospective effect of a building warranty deed.

enrichment.short_title: Building warranty deed held to take retrospective effect from practical completion for limitation purposes

statutes_considered.title: Limitation Act 1980
provisions: 12-year limitation period for actions on deeds under seal

key_facts: Northern & Shell plc, successor to the original leaseholder Stockley Academy Ltd, claimed defects in cladding and weatherproofing at Northern & Shell Tower, Millwall Dock.
John Laing Construction Ltd had entered a Deed of Warranty dated 16 January 1990 covenanting compliance with the JCT building contract for Merchants House.
Clause 5 provided that the deed should come into effect on the day following issue of the certificate of practical completion, which was 26 August 1989.
The deed was signed about four and a half months after practical completion but clause 5 was not amended.
If the cause of action accrued on 26 August 1989 the 12-year limitation period had expired when proceedings began; if on 16 January 1990 it had not.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment granted to the contractor on the basis that warranty claims were statute barred.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's conclusion that clause 5 operated retrospectively and the claims were time-barred was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a deed under seal expressly provides that it shall come into effect on the day after practical completion, the parties' intention—read in the factual matrix of the building contract requiring collateral warranties—was that the deed should operate retrospectively from that date, so limitation began to run from practical completion rather than from execution of the deed.
legal_issues: When the cause of action under the Deed of Warranty accrued for limitation purposes
Whether clause 5 had retrospective effect
Whether a pre-existing relationship between warrantor and warranty holder was necessary for retrospectivity
Whether section 56 of the Law of Property Act 1925 gave the leaseholder enforceable rights under the building contract

enrichment.short_title: Theft convictions upheld for removing abandoned golf balls from club water hazard
key_facts: Terry Rostron and John Mark Collinson were found at Whetstone golf club in diving suits with wet golf balls recovered from a water hazard after a burglar alarm alert.
They were convicted at Leicester Crown Court of theft and going equipped for theft.
The defence was that balls abandoned by players in the lake could not be property belonging to another.
The club professional gave evidence that balls lost in the lake after the permitted search time were surrendered to the club and could not be taken by unauthorised persons on the course.
There were no notices expressly claiming ownership of found balls, but the prosecution case rested on club practice and rules.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge; sentence appeals had already succeeded in part.
enrichment.ratio: On the facts there was sufficient evidence that golf balls in a club water hazard were property belonging to the club for Theft Act purposes, and a straightforward direction that the prosecution must prove the defendant knew he was not entitled to remove the balls satisfied the dishonesty requirement without a Ghosh direction.
legal_issues: Whether abandoned golf balls in a club lake remained property belonging to another under section 5 of the Theft Act 1968
Whether there was no case to answer on ownership
Whether the trial judge should have given a Ghosh direction on dishonesty

notes: Complete Commercial Court trial judgment on reinsurance avoidance for non-disclosure and misrepresentation.

enrichment.short_title: London reinsurers entitled to avoid Colombian bank reinsurance after non-disclosure of president's suspension
key_facts: London reinsurers sought declarations that they had validly avoided primary and excess bankers blanket bond and professional indemnity reinsurances covering Colombian state bank Caja Agraria for 1997/98 and a two-month 1998 extension.

Before placement, extensive Colombian media reports and official investigations concerned president Benjamin Medina's suspension, arrest, and alleged involvement in irregular loans of about 11 billion pesos.
At a London presentation in November 1997 the Colombian team gave a misleading partial explanation for Medina's absence, attributing suspension mainly to misuse of a company aeroplane.
Lead underwriter Mr Satterford was not told the full reasons; following underwriters received no disclosure of the suspension.
Claims later arose from irregular credits linked to the investigations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of reinsurers' claim for declarations of valid avoidance of reinsurance contracts.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeeded; non-disclosure and misrepresentation at placement and extension were material and induced underwriting; following market entitled to avoid.
enrichment.ratio: Allegations of serious misconduct against the president of the insured bank, supported by suspension, arrest and investigation, were material facts requiring disclosure to London reinsurers; partial misrepresentation about the reason for suspension induced the lead underwriter to write and extend the risk, and followers who relied on a fair presentation to the leader could also avoid.
legal_issues: Whether media reports and investigations were material to a prudent reinsurer
Whether the facts were presumed known to the reinsurer under section 18(3) of the Marine Insurance Act 1906
Whether non-disclosure and misrepresentation induced placement and extension
Whether the Discovery Limitation Clause narrowed disclosure obligations
Whether following underwriters could avoid by reason of non-disclosure to the lead underwriter

enrichment.short_title: Lawful development certificate refused for coal-yard to waste recycling change upheld as material change of use

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: Bennett Fergusson Coal Ltd sought a certificate of lawfulness of proposed use for a materials recycling facility on land at Grassmoor, Derbyshire, previously used for coal processing, screening, blending and distribution.
The inspector found both existing and proposed uses were sui generis rather than within Use Classes B2 or B8.
The proposed recycling operation would receive waste materials, sort and process them, and dispose of residue to landfill.
The inspector held a change from mineral/coal handling to waste recycling would be a material change of use in planning terms.
Derbyshire County Council had refused the certificate; the Secretary of State dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to an inspector's dismissal of an appeal against refusal of a certificate of lawfulness of proposed use.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the inspector was entitled to find a material change of use even if he had misdirected himself on whether the proposed recycling use fell within class B2.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a change of use is material is primarily a question of fact and degree for the decision-maker, assessed from a planning perspective; a change from established coal processing and distribution to a waste recycling/disposal service involving fundamentally different materials may properly be held material even where both operations include storage and processing elements.
legal_issues: Whether existing and proposed uses fell within the same use class under the 1987 Order
Whether the proposed recycling use was an industrial process within class B2
Whether change from coal yard use to materials recycling was a material change of use
Whether Article 3(6)(g) exclusion for mineral storage yards was relevant

notes: Complete joint Court of Appeal judgment in Munjaz and S on psychiatric seclusion.

enrichment.short_title: Mental Health Code of Practice on seclusion must be followed unless there is good reason to depart
key_facts: Colonel Munjaz challenged Ashworth Special Hospital's seclusion policy, which reduced medical reviews below the Mental Health Act Code of Practice and treated room-locking as seclusion.
Mr S challenged 12 days' seclusion at Airedale General Hospital in July-August 2001 while awaiting transfer to a secure unit.
The Code defines seclusion as supervised confinement to protect others from significant harm, to be used as a last resort and not as punishment or for staff shortage.
Sullivan J had treated the Code as mere guidance; Stanley Burnton J largely followed that approach in Mr S's case.
The court held seclusion is impliedly authorised by statutory detention powers and is capable of being medical treatment under section 63.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals from administrative court judgments on the lawfulness of hospital seclusion policies and individual seclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals allowed; Ashworth's wholesale departure from the Code was unlawful and Airedale was not justified in continuing Mr S's seclusion after it ceased to be necessary and proportionate.
enrichment.ratio: Hospitals must comply with the statutory Mental Health Act Code of Practice on seclusion unless they have good reason to depart in an individual case or for a properly defined group sharing relevant characteristics; length of seclusion alone cannot justify a general policy departure, and unjustified departure may render seclusion unlawful under public law and incompatible with Article 8 for lack of legality.
legal_issues: The domestic source and limits of the power to seclude detained psychiatric patients
Whether seclusion is medical treatment under section 63
The status and weight of the Code of Practice under section 118
Whether seclusion can breach Articles 3, 5 or 8 of the ECHR
Whether issue estoppel applies to judicial review of a revised hospital policy
catchwords: Mental Health Act Code of Practice

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on internal relocation in asylum cases.

enrichment.short_title: Internal relocation to Colombo held not unduly harsh test for refugee status where wife's PTSD was neutral factor
key_facts: AE and his wife, Sri Lankan Tamils from Jaffna, claimed asylum after clandestine entry; the husband had assisted the LTTE and been ill-treated in army detention.

An adjudicator found the husband had a well-founded fear of persecution in the north but not in Colombo, yet allowed both appeals because relocation to Colombo would be unduly harsh given the wife's PTSD after rape.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal held medical conditions alone do not make someone a refugee if adequate treatment exists in the internal relocation area.
The Court of Appeal reconsidered Robinson and the unduly harsh test in light of the Human Rights Act 1998.
Fresh psychiatric evidence was rejected because the appeal was on law alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on points of law from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision restoring the Secretary of State's refusal of asylum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the family were not refugees because they could reasonably be expected to relocate to Colombo despite the wife's psychiatric condition.
enrichment.ratio: When assessing internal relocation under the Refugee Convention, the unduly harsh test compares conditions in the area where persecution is feared with those in the safe haven, not with conditions in the country of asylum; a family member's psychiatric condition unrelated to Convention persecution is ordinarily a neutral factor and does not establish refugee status, though it may support separate human rights or humanitarian leave.
legal_issues: The correct approach to internal relocation under Article 1A(2) of the Refugee Convention
The meaning and application of the unduly harsh test from Robinson
Whether the protection limb of Article 1A(2) requires Convention-level rights in the relocation area
Whether the wife's PTSD made relocation unduly harsh

enrichment.short_title: Prior Customs seizure fax admissible to prove knowing involvement in cigarette duty evasion
key_facts: Czyzewski was convicted with two co-defendants of being knowingly concerned in fraudulently evading duty on cigarettes hidden in plastic pipes imported via Immingham and Felixstowe in July 2001.
Surveillance linked him to co-accused near the Birmingham delivery unit on 24 July 2001, though he was not among those arrested at delivery.
A fax dated 20 June 2000 from Ferryline Trailers to the appellant reported Customs seizure of over 2.5 million cigarettes hidden in timber consigned to his company Eurominute Ltd.
The appellant did not give evidence; the central issue was whether he knowingly participated in the 2001 importation.
The trial judge initially misdirected the jury on the fax but corrected the direction after lunch, explaining it went to knowledge in 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge following trial at Birmingham Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: Evidence of a prior Customs seizure fax in the defendant's possession, showing he knew cigarettes had previously been concealed in his company's import consignments, was admissible and relevant to whether he knowingly participated in the later fraudulent evasion of duty, provided the jury were directed that it went to knowledge rather than proof of the 2001 offences themselves.
legal_issues: Admissibility of the 2000 Customs seizure fax as evidence of knowledge
Whether the summing-up adequately corrected an initial misdirection on the fax
Whether the conviction was unsafe

notes: Complete section 288 judgment quashing inconsistent planning appeal decision.

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal quashed where second inspector failed to explain departure from earlier five-dwelling approval
key_facts: JS Bloor sought outline planning permission for five detached dwellings at Shimpling Street, Suffolk, on a site with a 1997 outline permission for chalet bungalows.
Inspector Goodman had determined a similar full application in December 2001, accepting the principle of five dwellings and low density as broadly acceptable.
Inspector Brown dismissed a renewed outline application in February 2003 mainly because density at 9.1 dwellings per hectare conflicted with PPG3 and emerging policy HS11 requiring 30-50 dph.
Brown also questioned the principle of development and suggested reassessment through the local plan process.
The council had not raised density or principle objections at the earlier appeal despite an identical planning policy background.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 to an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; inspector's decision quashed and remitted to a fresh inspector.
enrichment.ratio: A previous materially indistinguishable appeal decision on the same site is a material consideration requiring explicit reasons if a later inspector departs from it; failure adequately to explain departure from an earlier acceptance of development principle and density, together with an unjustified prematurity finding on a small village infill site, renders the later decision unlawful.
legal_issues: Weight to be given to a previous inspector's decision on the same site
Whether PPG3 density policy superseded adopted local plan policy LP16
Whether the inspector dismissed the appeal on prematurity grounds
Whether Structure Plan policy CS3 related to density
Whether the 5-6% population increase was a significant increase

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt hotel-to-flats scheme refused for lack of very special circumstances despite landscape gains
key_facts: Mr Lanni applied to demolish Bridge House Hotel near Reigate and replace it with 23 flats with parking and landscaping.
The site lies in the Metropolitan Green Belt, Surrey Hills AONB and an Area of Great Landscape Value, outside the defined urban area.
Council officers recommended approval but the planning committee refused; the inspector dismissed the appeal.
The inspector accepted the proposal would improve building design and conserve AONB/AGLV landscape character, but found inappropriate Green Belt development without very special circumstances.
He also held the site was poorly connected to services and public transport, making high-density housing unsustainable under PPG3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 to an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Inappropriate development in the Green Belt requires very special circumstances clearly outweighing harm from inappropriateness; visual and landscape improvements, even if they conserve AONB/AGLV character, may be insufficient on their own where the proposal remains inappropriate Green Belt development and lacks sustainable access to services.
legal_issues: Whether the proposal was inappropriate Green Belt development under PPG2
Whether very special circumstances existed to outweigh Green Belt harm
Whether procedural fairness was breached at the inquiry
Whether flats at proposed density were consistent with the locality
Whether travel-pattern evidence supported sustainability under PPG3

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on alternative pleading and employer negligence at loading dock.

enrichment.short_title: Claimant allowed to rely on defendant's account after disbelieved evidence; 50% contributory negligence
key_facts: Justin Binks, a Securicor van loader, fell from a box van at a Leeds warehouse loading dock on 15 October 1999.
He claimed the van moved while he was retracting the conveyor belt; Securicor said he was riding the belt contrary to notices and panicked when the rear door moved.
The trial judge preferred Securicor's accident-book account recorded by Mr Tovey and refused to let Binks run an alternative case based on that account.
Undisturbed findings established supervisor Watson signalled the driver to move off while Binks remained in the van.
Full-liability damages would have been £27,000 on the judge's quantum findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Leeds County Court after trial judge refused alternative case at close of evidence and dismissed the claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; alternative negligence case established with 50% contributory negligence, substituting judgment for £13,500.
enrichment.ratio: CPR Part 22 does not prevent a claimant from advancing an alternative factual case based on the opponent's evidence where there is an evidential foundation, and the court may permit amendment without a statement of truth where appropriate; where a supervisor orders a van to move while a worker remains inside, employer negligence is established even if the worker was also foolhardy in riding the conveyor belt.
legal_issues: Whether Part 22 barred pleading an alternative case inconsistent with the claimant's evidence
Whether the trial judge erred in refusing to permit the alternative case at trial
Whether Securicor was prejudiced by the late alternative case
Liability and contributory negligence on the alternative facts
